query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoparticle stability under high‐temperature catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions is governed by the presence of a buffering anion sublattice (e.g., an engineered surface oxide) that limits atomic diffusion and phase segregation, thereby preserving the single-phase, near-equiatomic solid solution.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles synthesized with a uniform metal distribution and a thin, naturally or intentionally formed oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, pre-formed oxide (buffering anion sublattice) on one set of nanoparticles while maintaining a minimal or absent oxide layer on a control set using inert-atmosphere synthesis.
generation.conditions: Exposure to high-temperature service regimes typical of catalytic operation (773–1173 K) or thermoelectric use (473–1923 K), including redox cycling conditions where the environment alternates between oxidative and reductive atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: A buffering oxide sublayer that acts as a diffusion barrier and stabilizer of the local chemical order.
generation.mechanism: The buffering oxide sublattice reduces the mobility of constituent metal atoms at high temperatures by providing a physical and chemical barrier to diffusion. This suppression of atomic diffusion limits phase segregation and elemental redistribution, thereby maintaining the integrity of the single-phase solid solution even under thermally or chemically stressful conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with the controlled oxide layer will exhibit higher structural and chemical stability (evidenced by preserved phase homogeneity and reduced elemental segregation) and superior performance in catalysis and thermoelectric applications compared to nanoparticles lacking this oxide layer.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized without intentional formation of a buffering oxide layer, which are expected to undergo more pronounced phase degradation and elemental segregation under identical service conditions.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism should be significant in systems where an anion sublattice is either inherent or can be engineered; however, in environments that are strictly inert or in systems where oxide formation is energetically unfavorable, the effect may be diminished.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of the buffering oxide on diffusion rates and its universal applicability across different alloy compositions and nanoparticle sizes remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two comparable sets of near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles: one set will receive a controlled oxidation treatment to establish a buffering oxide layer while the other will be synthesized and maintained under inert conditions to minimize oxide formation. Both sets will then be subjected to cyclic high-temperature treatments and redox environments simulating catalytic/thermoelectric operation.
measurements: Phase analysis and homogeneity via X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Elemental mapping and microstructural analysis via transmission electron microscopy coupled with energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (TEM-EDS)
Surface chemistry and oxidation states via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
Performance stability evaluations in catalytic or thermoelectric activity tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with the engineered oxide layer do not demonstrate statistically significant improvement in phase stability, reduced elemental segregation, or operational performance relative to the inert-synthesized nanoparticles, the role of the buffering anion sublattice in governing stability will be refuted.

Sub-nanometric High-Entropy Alloy Cluster: Hydrogen Spillover Driven Synthesis on CeO2 and Structural Reversibility

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (NPs) have attracted significant attention as promising catalysts owing to the various unique synergistic effects originating from the nanometer-scale, near-equimolar mixing of five or more components to produce single-phase solid solutions. However, the study of sub-nanometer HEA clusters having sizes of less than 1 nm remains incomplete despite the possibility of novel functions related to borderline molecular states with discrete quantum energy levels. The present work demonstrates the synthesis of CeO2 nanorods (CeO2-NRs) on which sub-nanometer CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters were formed with the aid of a pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on readily reducible CeO2 (110) facets. The CoNiCuZnPd HEA sub-nanoclusters exhibited higher activity during the reduction of NO by H2 even at low temperatures compared with the corresponding monometallic catalysts. (Mg,Mn,Fe,Co,Ni)O: A rocksalt high-entropy oxide containing divalent Mn and Fe

Abstract: High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. A PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy alloy nanocatalyst for the hydrogenation of nitrobenzene†

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple elements in near-equiatomic proportions hold great promise in heterogeneous catalysis because of their exceptional physicochemical properties governed by synergy. Herein, we prepared PtPdCoCuNi HEA nanoparticles via a one-step colloid-based route and tested their catalytic performance for nitrobenzene hydrogenation to aniline. The SiO2 supported PtPdCoCuNi displays 93.9% yield of aniline at 80 °C, which is 2.11 times that of PtPd/SiO2. Even at room temperature, a 47.4% yield of aniline is attained with the PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst. DRIFTS experiments indicate formation of isolated Pt and Pd sites after alloying the transition metals and evidence a stronger interaction between the HEA catalyst and nitrobenzene. Both XPS data and DFT calculations disclose charge transfer to Pt and Pd species, which eventually enhance the interaction between nitrobenzene and the isolated metal sites and the hydrogenation activity as well.
